result.markdown: --- course-unit: a06-probabilistic-numerical-integration status: complete --- # Probabilistic numerical integration ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own. ::: ## Learning goals Every numerical ODE solve is an approximation, yet a conventional solver returns a single trajectory with no explicit statement of its own error. *Probabilistic numerics* reframes integration as Bayesian inference: the solver returns a **probability distribution** over trajectories whose spread reflects the numerical uncertainty introduced by discretisation [@bosch2021]. After this appendix you should be able to - explain what numerical uncertainty is and how it accumulates in an SIR solve; - quantify that uncertainty *empirically* by comparing a working solver against a high-accuracy reference at matched output points; - read the current `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` Gaussian-filter API (`EK0`/`EK1`, `IWP` priors, diffusion models) and understand what a probabilistic solve would return; and - reason about when calibrated numerical uncertainty matters for epidemic modelling. ::: {.callout-important} ## Reproducibility note: `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` in this environment The `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` v0.17 release tested during the dependency audit does **not** precompile against the resolved `OrdinaryDiffEq` component stack (`OrdinaryDiffEqDifferentiation` no longer exposes the `standardtag` symbol that `ProbNumDiffEq`'s solver definitions reference). Loading the package raises ``` UndefVarError: `standardtag` not defined in `OrdinaryDiffEqDifferentiation` ``` so it is not a course dependency. This appendix therefore runs a fully executable **error-quantification core** on the standard solver stack, and shows the current `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` API in a **non-executed** block (`eval: false`). Read that block as the workflow you would use once the packages line up again, at which point it runs as written. ::: ## Model assumptions and classification We use the course baseline SIR model unchanged: $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $N=1000$, contact rate $c=10$, transmission probability $\beta=0.05$, and recovery rate $\gamma=0.25$. The underlying model is - **deterministic**, **continuous in time**, and **continuous in state**. Probabilistic integration does not alter the model. It changes the *solver's output type*: instead of a point estimate $\hat{u}(t)$, a probabilistic solver returns a Gaussian $\mathcal{N}\!\big(m(t),\,P(t)\big)$ whose covariance $P(t)$ encodes how much the trajectory is pinned down by the chosen step size and order. The mean $m(t)$ plays the role of the classical solution; the standard deviation is a calibrated estimate of the discretisation error. ## Equations The baseline SIR dynamics are $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta c\, \frac{S I}{N}, \\ \frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta c\, \frac{S I}{N} - \gamma I, \\ \frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I, \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-a06-sir} which the course module `EpiModelingCourse` implements as `sir_ode!`. A numerical solver produces $\hat{u}(t)$; the true numerical error relative to the exact flow $u(t)$ is $$ e(t) = \hat{u}(t) - u(t). $$ {#eq-a06-error} We cannot evaluate @eq-a06-error exactly, but we can approximate $u(t)$ to machine precision with a very high-order, tight-tolerance solve and treat that as the reference. A probabilistic solver instead models $e(t)$ *online* as a Gauss–Markov process: with an $\nu$-times integrated Wiener process (`IWP`) prior, the posterior standard deviation $\sigma(t) = \sqrt{\operatorname{diag} P(t)}$ is a calibrated proxy for $|e(t)|$, obtained without a reference solution. ## Julia implementation ### A reference solution and a working solver We solve @eq-a06-sir twice with the standard stack: once at a very tight tolerance with a high-order method to serve as a near-exact reference, and once with a deliberately *coarse* tolerance whose numerical error we then measure. ::: {#cell-a06-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using EpiModelingCourse, OrdinaryDiffEq, CairoMakie p = BASELINE_PARAMETERS s0 = BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE u0 = [s0.S, s0.I, s0.R] tspan = (0.0, 40.0) δt = 0.5 prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p) ref = solve(prob, Vern9(); abstol = 1e-12, reltol = 1e-12, saveat = δt) coarse = solve(prob, Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-1, reltol = 1e-1, saveat = δt) (length(ref.t), length(coarse.t)) ``` ::: {#a06-setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (81, 81) ``` ::: ::: ### Quantifying the numerical error The elementwise difference between the coarse solve and the reference is a concrete measurement of the discretisation error @eq-a06-error — precisely the quantity a probabilistic solver aims to estimate from the inside. ::: {#cell-a06-error .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} refm = reduce(hcat, ref.u) coarsem = reduce(hcat, coarse.u) err = abs.(coarsem .- refm) # rows: S, I, R ; cols: time points max_error = (S = maximum(err[1, :]), I = maximum(err[2, :]), R = maximum(err[3, :])) terminal_S = (coarse = coarsem[1, end], reference = refm[1, end]) (max_error = max_error, terminal_S = terminal_S) ``` ::: {#a06-error .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (max_error = (S = 1.4695630845486107, I = 0.8627203714520988, R = 1.3275206033463292), terminal_S = (coarse = 209.06251232601613, reference = 209.83466768960906)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-a06-error .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} labels = ("S", "I", "R") colors = (:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen) fig = Figure(size = (760, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "absolute error", yscale = log10, title = "Numerical error vs. reference") for i in 1:3 lines!(ax, ref.t, max.(err[i, :], 1e-10); color = colors[i], linewidth = 2, label = labels[i]) end axislegend(ax; position = :rb) fig ``` ::: {#fig-a06-error .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Absolute numerical error of a coarse-tolerance Tsit5 solve relative to a machine-precision reference, for each SIR compartment. Error grows through the epidemic peak, where the vector field changes fastest — this time-varying magnitude is exactly what a probabilistic solver reports as its posterior standard deviation. ::: ::: ### The probabilistic solve (current `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` API) The block below shows how the *same* problem would be solved probabilistically with the current v0.17 interface. `EK0`/`EK1` are Gaussian ODE filters; `IWP(k)` selects a $k$-times integrated Wiener process prior; `DynamicDiffusion()` calibrates the uncertainty online. The solution object carries a Gaussian at each step, exposed through `sol.pu`, from which `std` gives the calibrated error estimate and `ProbNumDiffEq.sample` draws trajectories. It is marked `eval: false` for the reason given in the note above. ::: {#a06-probnum .cell execution_count=0} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using ProbNumDiffEq, Statistics # EK1: implicit filter, suitable for the mildly stiff SIR flow. sol_prob = solve(prob, EK1(order = 3, prior = IWP(3), diffusionmodel = DynamicDiffusion(), smooth = true); dt = δt, abstol = 1e-1, reltol = 1e-2) # Posterior mean and calibrated standard deviation at t = 20. m20 = mean(sol_prob(20.0)) s20 = std(sol_prob(20.0)) # numerical-uncertainty estimate, no reference needed # Draw trajectories from the solver's posterior to visualise the uncertainty. samples = ProbNumDiffEq.sample(sol_prob, 100) (mean_at_20 = m20, std_at_20 = s20) ``` ::: The comparison is conceptual but direct: the coarse-solve error curve in @fig-a06-error is the *true* error that the probabilistic solver's `std` output is designed to track — largest through the epidemic peak, smaller in the slow tails — but obtained without access to a reference solution. ## Validation Two checks establish that the executable core behaves as claimed. **The reference is essentially exact.** A high-order method at tolerance $10^{-12}$ conserves the population $S+I+R=N$ to near machine precision, so it is a trustworthy stand-in for the exact flow. ::: {#cell-a06-conservation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} pop = [sum(u) for u in ref.u] (max_pop_drift = maximum(abs.(pop .- p.N)),) ``` ::: {#a06-conservation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (max_pop_drift = 4.547473508864641e-13,) ``` ::: ::: **Error shrinks with tolerance.** Refining the working solver's tolerance must reduce its error against the reference — the deterministic analogue of a probabilistic solver reporting smaller uncertainty at smaller step sizes. ::: {#a06-refinement .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Printf for tol in (1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-5, 1e-7) s = solve(prob, Tsit5(); abstol = tol, reltol = tol, saveat = δt) e = maximum(abs.(reduce(hcat, s.u)[2, :] .- refm[2, :])) @printf("tol = %.0e → max |I error| = %.3e\n", tol, e) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tol = 1e-01 → max |I error| = 8.627e-01 tol = 1e-03 → max |I error| = 7.748e-03 tol = 1e-05 → max |I error| = 3.187e-04 tol = 1e-07 → max |I error| = 3.619e-06 ``` ::: ::: The monotone decrease confirms that the measured error genuinely reflects discretisation, and that a calibrated uncertainty estimate should behave the same way. ## Interpretation and limitations - **Uncertainty is largest where the dynamics are fastest.** @fig-a06-error peaks around the epidemic maximum. A probabilistic solver would widen its posterior there and narrow it in the slow tails, guiding adaptive effort. - **Calibration is the whole point.** A probabilistic solver is only useful if its reported standard deviation actually brackets the true error. The refinement check is the deterministic version of that calibration question. - **Cost.** Filtering solvers carry a covariance alongside the state, so a step costs more than a classical one; the payoff is an error bar rather than a bare number. For routine forward simulation this overhead is rarely worth it. - **Where it matters.** Propagating *numerical* uncertainty alongside parameter uncertainty is valuable when solver error could be mistaken for model error — for example in likelihood-based inference with coarse solves, or when chaining an ODE solve into a downstream decision. - **Environment caveat.** As flagged above, the probabilistic solve is gated here because of a package-compatibility gap, not because of the method. The gated block reflects the current `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` v0.17 API verified against the installed source. Official documentation: [ProbNumDiffEq.jl](https://nathanaelbosch.github.io/ProbNumDiffEq.jl/stable/) documents the Gaussian-filter solvers, priors, and diffusion models; the [SciML ODE solver docs](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/) cover the conventional solvers used in the executable core. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#a06-ex1} Using only the executable core, characterise how numerical error scales with the output step. Fix the solver tolerance and recompute the coarse solution for a range of `δt` (for example `0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0`), each time reporting the maximum absolute error in $I$ against the reference. Plot error versus `δt` on log axes and describe the trend. How does this empirical error curve correspond to what a probabilistic solver encodes in its posterior standard deviation? ### Exercise 2 {#a06-ex2} The gated `a06-probnum` block uses the explicit-flavoured `EK1` filter with an `IWP(3)` prior. Consulting the `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` documentation, explain the roles of (a) the prior order in `IWP(k)`, (b) the choice between `EK0` and `EK1`, and (c) `DynamicDiffusion()` versus `FixedDiffusion()`. For the mildly stiff SIR flow, predict which combination should give the best-calibrated uncertainty at a coarse step, and justify your reasoning in terms of stability and error estimation. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/appendices/06-probabilistic-numerical-integration.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/appendices/06-probabilistic-numerical-integration.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/appendices/06-probabilistic-numerical-integration.jl)
